items.title: LRMoE: Demand-Side Load Re-Calibration for Efficient MoE Training on Memory-Constrained Nodes
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37720v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer scalable capacity for Web applications, but uneven routing creates computation and communication bottlenecks. Existing placement and replication methods redistribute this workload, yet additional expert copies compete with token-related buffers for limited GPU memory. We present LRMoE, a memory-aware MoE training system that jointly recalibrates backward demand and balances the retained workload. During forward execution, it plans retention quotas and expert placement under resource constraints while preserving all routed computations. During backpropagation, a load recalibration metric estimates each token-expert pair's contribution to the expert update and selects pairs within these quotas. A capacity-aware routing algorithm distributes retained pairs among eligible instances of their original experts. Physical compaction then forms smaller communication payloads and variable-size grouped GEMMs, reducing backward traffic, computation, and execution-buffer demand. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and GLM4.5-106B-A12B show that LRMoE reduces cumulative MoE-layer training time to fixed-loss tar

items.title: Amortized Localized Posterior Inference for Model Calibration with Application to an Ocean Turbulence Closure
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37731v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Model discrepancy may prevent a single calibration parameter from reproducing a physical response across the context domain. In addition, uncertainties in observations and contexts affect calibration and must be accounted for and quantified. We construct a family of localized posteriors by weighting observation likelihoods according to their proximity to a target context. Gaussian localization weights incorporate context uncertainty through covariance inflation, with reflection at domain boundaries and an optional correction for uneven context sampling. A conditional normalizing flow approximates the family of posteriors through amortized variational inference. Integrating the localized posteriors under a prescribed context measure gives the marginalized parameter distribution. In a twin experiment with the Branin-Hoo model, we compare global and localized inference under uniform and skewed context distributions. Localization reduces the reported aggregate predictive errors relative to the global posterior. items.title: ThinkJev: One Thought, Every Budget for Calibrated Typed Decisions
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37732v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many uses of language models end in a typed decision: a choice among a closed set of options, whose probabilities code can act on. Reading those probabilities from one forward pass is fast but often wrong on decisions that take several steps, such as arithmetic, counting, and date comparison. Letting the model think first fixes most of these errors, but costs seconds per decision instead of milliseconds. To pay for thinking only where it helps, ThinkJev builds a fast and a slow system from one open hybrid-thinking model that can answer directly or after a thought. System 1 reads the model's probabilities for the option letters when it answers directly; System 2 reads the same letters after the model has thought on the same cached prompt, so escalating repeats no work and both systems give probabilities over the same options. Because the letters can be read after any number of thought tokens, one sampled thought also gives the answer under every thinking budget. Without training, ThinkJev lets System 1 answer alone only where a statistical test on labeled dev data guarantees that its accepted answers stay under a target error rate. At

items.title: OpenFrontiers: A Collection of Open Research Problems and a Benchmark for Scientific Rediscovery
items.excerpt: arXiv:2610.37739v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean~4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. items.title: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 2x RTX 5090 with 504 tok/s decode: QEngine 1.3.1 decodes ~1.5-1.9x faster than the next-best engine I've tried (numbers, caveats, and what still bites)
items.excerpt: https://github.com/bpx03/QEngine (not my repo, credit goes to bpx03) QEngine was built for 3x RTX 3090s. I was able to compile for RTX 5090s. I've now run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on the same box through four different engines. QEngine (bpx03, v1.3.1) is the fastest for single-stream decode by a clear margin, level with Strata on agentic prompt latency, and it has a KV-in-RAM mode that makes returning to idle conversations much cheaper. Details below, including the parts that make it look less good. Rig: 2x RTX 5090 (32 GB each), Threadripper PRO 3975WX, 251 GB RAM, 262K context. QEngine's INT4 AutoRound build of Flash-Next. The README only lists sm_86, so I built it for sm_120 by changing CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES from 86 to 120 (nvcc 13.3, g++-13). No other changes. It's up and serving 53 s after launch. Speed (club-3090 bench.sh , same script and prompts for every engine) Engine / quant Decode narrative / code (tok/s) Prefill @10K / @90K (tok/s) QEngine 1.3.1 (KV in VRAM, default) 370 / 439 ~5.7K / ~7.3K QEngine 1.3.1 ( FLASH_KV=ram ) 406 / 504 ~6.2K @10K Strata ISTA IQ3_S 214 / 293 ~5.1K / ~10.0K
items.summary: https://github.com/bpx03/QEngine (not my repo, credit goes to bpx03) QEngine was built for 3x RTX 3090s. I was able to compile for RTX 5090s.
